title: David and Goliath: The Battle Is the LORD's
summary: The Philistine champion Goliath of Gath taunts Israel's army in the Valley of Elah for forty days, and Saul and his soldiers are paralyzed by fear. David, sent by his father with food for his brothers, hears the giant defy "the armies of the living God," volunteers to fight him, refuses Saul's armor, and goes out with a sling and five stones. He strikes Goliath down in the name of the LORD, Israel routs the Philistines, and Saul asks whose son this young man is.
story: Chapter 16 anointed David in private and brought him into Saul's court as a musician. Chapter 17 makes him known to all Israel. The chapter tests the words spoken at his anointing, that the LORD does not look on outward appearance: the tallest, best-armed man on the field is defeated by a shepherd boy. It also sharpens the contrast with Saul, the man who stood head and shoulders above everyone else (10:23), who was chosen to fight Israel's battles (8:20), and who now hides in his tent while a boy does the fighting. From here David's fame begins to grow, and so does Saul's jealousy.
historical:
The Valley of Elah runs west from the hill country of Judah toward the Philistine plain, a natural corridor for Philistine attempts to push inland. Socoh and Azekah, named in verse 1, are known sites overlooking the valley, and Gath, Goliath's city, has been identified with Tell es-Safi, where excavations have uncovered a large Philistine city. Nearby, the fortified site of Khirbet Qeiyafa, excavated from 2007, dates to roughly the time of Saul and David; its excavators proposed identifying it with the Shaaraim of verse 52, though that identification is debated.

The chapter raises several historical and textual questions. Goliath's height is six cubits and a span in the traditional Hebrew text, about nine and a half feet; the Dead Sea Scrolls copy of Samuel and the Greek translation read four cubits and a span, about six and a half feet, still a giant among men of that day. The oldest Greek manuscripts also lack much of verses 12 to 31 and 55 to 58, which suggests the chapter circulated in more than one form. Elsewhere, 2 Samuel 21:19 credits a man named Elhanan with killing Goliath of Gath, while 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan killed Goliath's brother; scholars explain the relation of these texts in different ways. Verse 54 says David brought the head to Jerusalem, which was not yet an Israelite city; many take this as the narrator anticipating what David would later do there.
cultural:
Single combat between champions was a known practice in the ancient world, a way to decide a battle, or at least to shame the other side, without a full clash of armies. Goliath's challenge in verses 8 and 9 follows that pattern. His equipment is described in unusual detail: a bronze helmet, scale armor weighing five thousand shekels (roughly 125 pounds), bronze greaves, a javelin, and a spear with a shaft like a weaver's beam. The detail is meant to impress, and it also shows the Philistine advantage in metal that 13:19-22 described.

The sling was not a child's toy. Trained slingers were a regular part of ancient armies (Judges 20:16 describes seven hundred left-handed Benjamite slingers who could hit a hair), and a smooth stone thrown hard could kill at a distance. A shepherd would have used a sling to defend the flock. Calling the Philistines "uncircumcised" marked them as outside the covenant, since circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham's family (Genesis 17). Saul's reward of wealth, a royal marriage, and tax exemption for the victor's family was the kind of royal favor a champion could expect.
literary: This is one of the longest single episodes in Samuel, told with patient, dramatic pacing. It opens with a wide view of two armies on two hills, then narrows to one giant, then to one boy. Goliath is described at length and speaks first; David speaks last and longest. The key word is "defy" or "taunt," repeated by Goliath, the soldiers, and David; what the soldiers hear as a threat to Israel, David hears as an insult to the living God. The contrast between Saul's armor and David's shepherd equipment is deliberate, and so is the contrast between Goliath's curses by his gods and David's speech in the name of the LORD of Hosts (verses 45 to 47), which is the theological center of the chapter. The ending, with Saul asking whose son David is, turns the story toward the question of David's family and his future place in the kingdom.

outline.t: Two armies face each other across the Valley of Elah
Jesse sends David to his brothers at the camp
David asks about the giant; Eliab's anger
David before Saul: lions, bears, and borrowed armor
The exchange of words: in the name of the LORD
Goliath falls and the Philistines flee
Saul asks whose son David is

doctrines.note: David calls the LORD "the living God" and speaks so that "the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel." The contest is really between the LORD and the gods Goliath curses by, and the point is God's reputation among the nations.

David tells the assembled armies that "it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves," and that "the battle is the LORD’s." Deliverance does not depend on human strength or equipment. God saves, and he often does so through unlikely instruments.
David's courage rests on past experience of God's faithfulness: the LORD who delivered him from lion and bear will deliver him now. Faith here is memory put to work in a new danger.

words.note: Charaph, to taunt, defy, or reproach. Goliath uses it of Israel's ranks; David uses it of "the armies of the living God." A related noun is translated "disgrace" in verse 26. The word frames the whole contest as a question of honor: whose God will be shamed?

Benayim, champion, literally a man of the between, the one who steps into the space between two armies. The word is used only here in the Old Testament, and it captures the idea of single combat: one man representing his people.

Chay, living or alive. David twice calls the LORD "the living God" (verses 26 and 36), in contrast to the Philistine gods, which cannot act. The same title is used when Israel first crossed into the land (Joshua 3:10).

Yasha, to save. In verse 47 David says the LORD does not save by sword or spear. The verb connects this victory with Jonathan's words in 14:6 and with the whole Old Testament picture of God as the one who rescues his people.

christ: Readers have long seen in this chapter a pattern that finds its fullest meaning in Christ, though the chapter itself is a battle story, not an allegory. David stands as Israel's representative, a champion who fights on behalf of a people too afraid to fight, and his victory becomes theirs. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who defeats the enemies his people could not face, sin and death and the powers behind them, and shares his victory with them (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14-15). The difference matters: most readers are not David in this story but the frightened soldiers on the hillside, delivered by another. The chapter also sets out a principle the gospel makes plainer still, that God saves not by the world's weapons but through weakness, and that the victory is his.

hard.q: Why does Saul ask who David is when David was already his harpist and armor-bearer in chapter 16?
hard.a: Readers have noticed this for centuries. Several explanations are offered. Some suggest that Saul, tormented and distracted, simply did not recognize or remember a young court musician, or that David had been home with the flocks long enough to have grown and changed. Others point out that Saul asks whose son David is, not his name: with a royal marriage and a tax exemption promised to the victor's family, Saul may be asking about David's father and household. Many scholars instead think the chapter preserves two accounts of how David came to Saul's attention, which the editor placed side by side; the shorter form of the chapter in the oldest Greek manuscripts, which lacks verses 55 to 58, is sometimes cited in support. These readings are not all exclusive, and the text does not resolve the question. The story's main claims about God and David do not depend on which is right.

questions: The soldiers saw a giant and David saw an insult to the living God. How does what you believe about God change what you see in a crisis?
David refused armor he had not tested. When have you tried to serve God in someone else's armor, and what would it look like to use what God has actually given you?
David remembered the lion and the bear before he faced the giant. What past experiences of God's faithfulness could you recall in a present fear?
